prompt:
Research what the Python Software Foundation or the CPython developers have officially said about the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build. Cite the PEP or documentation page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

If you're not sure about something, just say so.

response.content:
The Python Software Foundation and CPython developers have outlined specific performance expectations and trade-offs for the free-threaded (no-GIL) build through PEP 703, PEP 779, and official documentation. The consensus is that while the free-threaded build incurs a performance penalty in single-threaded or linear benchmarks due to thread-safety overheads, this cost is considered acceptable given the benefits of true parallelism on multi-core systems.

Below are the specific statements regarding performance impact:

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "The performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks (for example as run by Microsoft’s Faster CPython team, or Meta’s Python Runtime team), is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it’s more like 3%)." | CLAIM: PEP 779 states that the current linear performance penalty for free-threaded Python is approximately 10% on most platforms, but only about 3% on macOS.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "We propose 15% as a hard performance target." | CLAIM: PEP 779 proposes a hard performance target of a 15% penalty for phase II of making free-threaded Python officially supported.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The changes to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL increase execution overhead for `--disable-gil` builds." | CLAIM: PEP 700 acknowledges that disabling the GIL introduces execution overhead due to the necessary thread-safety changes.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "On the pyperformance benchmark suite, the average overhead ranges from about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux systems." | CLAIM: The official Python documentation notes that single-threaded overhead varies by hardware, ranging from 1% on macOS ARM to 8% on Linux x86-64.

SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "At this point we’re expecting a (worst case) performance penalty of 10-15%." | CLAIM: The Steering Council indicated during the acceptance of PEP 703 that they anticipated a worst-case performance penalty between 10% and 15%.

SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "The performance impact should be isolated to a free-threaded build; a GIL build should not see any performance impact in existing code." | CLAIM: The Steering Council specified that the performance costs of free-threading must not affect the default GIL-enabled builds of CPython.

SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "The free-threaded build will typically use more memory compared to the default build." | CLAIM: The official documentation confirms that free-threaded Python typically consumes more memory than the standard GIL-enabled build.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "Free-threaded Python currently sees about 15-20% higher memory use (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance)." | CLAIM: PEP 779 quantifies the memory usage increase for free-threaded Python as approximately 15-20% higher than the GIL build.
